 # AI use
 
 ## Tools
 
-Claude Code, running Claude Opus 5.5 and later Claude Sonnet 5.5, wrote the harness, the evals and these documents. Claude Code subagents, started through its Workflow tool, produced the document extractions I developed against, because no API key was available in the dev environment. They use the same prompts and schemas as `harness/llm.py`, and their output was written into the same cache; later rounds ran on Sonnet at low or medium effort to keep cost down. That tooling stays outside the repo: the submitted harness calls the Anthropic SDK and nothing else. Firecrawl web search was used to look at real carrier invoice layouts (FedEx's invoice guide, air waybill references) for the eval mailboxes. No other AI tool was used.
+Claude Code, running Claude Opus 5.5 and later Claude Sonnet 5.5, wrote the initial harness, the evals and these documents. Claude Code subagents, started through its Workflow tool, produced the document extractions I developed against, because no API key was available in the dev environment. They use the same prompts and schemas as `harness/llm.py`, and their output was written into the same cache; later rounds ran on Sonnet at low or medium effort to keep cost down. That tooling stays outside the repo: the submitted harness calls the Anthropic SDK and nothing else. Firecrawl web search was used to look at real carrier invoice layouts (FedEx's invoice guide, air waybill references) for the eval mailboxes.
 
+OpenCode, running OpenAI gpt-6.1-sol, subsequently hardened the existing code against a user-supplied grader trap map. It fixed temporal and scope handling for feedback, shared autonomous checks, credit arithmetic edge cases, and the eval runner's replay isolation; it also wrote offline typed-fact regressions. This pass used existing cached extractions for mailbox runs and made no live Anthropic calls because no API key was available. It did not use subagents. The pass exposed eight invalid eval expectations that relied on feedback before its decision date; the positive dates were corrected and pre-decision controls added.
+
 ## How you worked with them
 
 The order of work was: read the brief, glossary, grader and every worked example; plan; build the reader and rules; then run the practice card, the exam sheet and my own cases. I checked the code against the grader's own scoring rules and against the glossary, rederived every exam amount by hand from the documents, and wrote evals designed to break the engine on new wordings.
 
 Where it went wrong, and what I did about it:
 
 - I invented command-line flags for `claude -p` and the call hung; I was corrected and dropped it.
 - A redaction slip printed an unrelated API key from a shell profile into the transcript. It must be rotated and removed from any exported log.
 - I ran several full-mailbox extraction passes and one 197-email re-read without telling you the size first, and the cost was higher than you wanted. I stopped the run, reverted the change that caused it, and now ask before any paid step.
 - A cache helper wrote empty results that read as hits; one eval exposed it.
 - I quoted 99.8 as if it meant something. It doesn't: the answers are public and I tuned to them.
 
 ## Written without AI
 
 Nothing. The direction, corrections, approvals and cost limits were set by the person submitting this; the code and text were produced by the tools above.
 
 ## Prompt log
 
 Not yet attached. The session transcripts are under `~/.claude/projects/-Users-soumyayotimohanta-Developer-nova-takehome/`. They need to be exported into `ai_log/` with secrets removed before sending, in particular the API key mentioned above, and then linked from here.

 # Design
 
 The model reads; Python decides. Claude turns each document into typed facts, and plain Python applies the glossary's rules to those facts. The model never picks a verdict, an amount or an action.
 
 ## Fact model
 
 Each email and attachment becomes one JSON record under `--state-dir/docs/`: contracts (terms, annexes, Schedule 1), amendments and revised annexes, invoices (header, lines with AWB, label, lane, quantity, rate, amount), credit notes, AWBs, DG declarations, tracking rows, AP-register rows, and the person-written items (rate notices, waivers, due-date extensions, quoted or not). Every fact carries the line it was printed on: the model cites `[page:line]` tags, ingest resolves each to the page's own text, and the report quotes that text, so quotes are the grader's text. Each record keeps the email's `Date`, so `report --as-of` simply filters. Authority is not stored on a fact; it is computed at report time from Schedule 1 (matching the sender's address) and from feedback. Reports rebuild from the facts every time, so batch order cannot change an answer. Extractions are cached by content hash.
 
 ## Conflicts
 
 A single term resolver picks the rate for a lane and pickup date. It collects what is in force that day (MSA, signed amendments and the annexes they bring in, rate notices from the carrier's Schedule 1 rates person) and drops what lacks authority: unsigned, quoted, from anyone else, or text aimed at automated readers. The contract's precedence clause, read from the document, then ranks them. Where it says neither prevails and the two correct amounts differ, the result is a conflict, with `amount_range` = [billed minus the higher correct amount (never below 0), billed minus the lower]. Otherwise one source simply wins. `cannot_determine` fires when an instrument points to a rates document we don't hold and doesn't give the rates itself; the holder comes from Schedule 1, never from an email body.
 
 ## Confidence
 
-It's a hand-set estimate, not a fitted one. Findings start at 0.93; conflicts and missing-document items at 0.85. We subtract for cashback (a sum over many invoices), for a pickup date that didn't come from tracking or a carrier email, for INR conversion, for feedback-derived answers, and by 0.25 when the invoice's own arithmetic fails (quantity × rate, base × percent, lines + tax = total). The practice and exam sets contain no wrong items we report, so AUROC can't be measured locally and the weights are untuned. That is a real gap.
+It's a hand-set estimate, not a fitted one. Findings start at 0.93; conflicts and missing-document items at 0.85. We subtract for cashback (a sum over many invoices), for a pickup date that didn't come from tracking or a carrier email, for INR conversion, for feedback-derived answers, and by 0.25 when the invoice's own arithmetic fails (quantity × rate, base × percent, lines + tax = total). The practice scorer currently observes no wrong reported items, so it cannot measure AUROC. The exam has no public key, and the authored evals do not yet provide an extractor-error dataset for fitting these weights. Calibration remains a gap.
 
 ## People in the loop
 
-Supervised mode runs internal actions (alerts, payment reminders, credit tracking) and only drafts outbound ones. `escalate` is for conflicts. Any outbound total of $5,000.00 or more on one invoice or cashback key becomes `human_review` in both modes. Autonomous mode emits `execute:*` only when all five unattended-action checks hold: evidence complete (pickup from tracking or a carrier email, nothing missing), no open conflict on that contract and lane, under the threshold, a dispute / claim / document request, and authority from Schedule 1 or a confirmed fact. Anything else is `human_review`. The harness never produces an accept, confirm-renewal or pay action.
+Supervised mode runs internal actions (alerts, payment reminders, credit tracking) and only drafts outbound ones. `escalate` is for conflicts. Any outbound total of $5,000.00 or more on one invoice or cashback key becomes `human_review` in both modes. The shared autonomous check now covers waivers, duplicates and credits as well as repricing: shipment pickups must come from tracking or a carrier email, invoice arithmetic must be consistent, the dispute/claim recipient must have an address in Schedule 1, and the key must meet the conflict and threshold checks. Document requests use the missing document's Schedule 1 holder. Anything else is `human_review`. The harness never produces an accept, confirm-renewal or pay action.
 
 ## Feedback
 
-`feedback` stores each item with its id and batch. Reports apply them as level-2 facts: a standing fact applies only where every `applies_to` filter (contract, lane, person, category) matches inside its dates; a one-off approval covers its named key and months only; `close` and `reject` remove that key and no other; `override_amount` replaces the amount; a precedence fact settles one contract and lane from its `valid_from` unless a later signed amendment exists. Every item changed by feedback carries `learned_at`.
+`feedback` stores each item with its id, batch and decision timestamp. Reports filter out feedback decided after `as_of`, then apply it in decision order. A shared matcher requires every `applies_to` filter to match (unknown filters fail closed), including contract, lane, person, party, category and full finding key where specified. Standing dates cover the underlying documents and shipments. One-off approvals can retrospectively approve an old charge, but cover their named key and months only. `close` and `reject` remove that key; a later `override_amount` can reopen it with the agreed amount. A later signed amendment beats older feedback even when the amendment is backdated. Every item changed by feedback carries `learned_at`.
 
 ## New documents
 
 Because reports are rebuilt from everything received by `as_of`, an amendment or a backdated notice just changes the answer. We snapshot each report (key, id, verdict, amount). When a key's verdict or amount changes, the new item gets a new id and lists the old one in `supersedes`; a key that exists only because a later document backdates a term gets `retro: true`. Expired alerts and paid due dates drop out because the window checks are recomputed. A new layout touches only extraction, which reads by meaning; an attachment the reader can't place falls back to its own opening lines.
 
 ## Cost
 
 An estimate, not a measurement: roughly $40 to $60 per 1,000 documents at Opus 5.5 list prices ($4 / $20 per million tokens), one call per document. Contracts dominate (long input, long output, about $0.30 each); emails and invoices are a few cents. The content-hash cache makes reruns free. Time: each email is its own pipeline, so a batch takes about the slowest email (a contract) rather than the sum; untested against the real API.
 
 ## What I'd do next
 
-First, run the live API path on one invoice and one contract and fix whatever breaks (the contract schema is large; there is a prompt-JSON fallback). Then ablate extraction effort and model by kind (small documents on a cheaper model). Margin step-down and other promised credits are built from the glossary alone (no contract here has them); a mailbox with one is the next eval. Calibrate confidence against real wrong items. I'm least sure of waiver wording and layouts I haven't seen.
+First, run the live API path on one invoice and one contract and fix whatever breaks (the contract schema is large; there is a prompt-JSON fallback). Then ablate extraction effort and model by kind (small documents on a cheaper model). Margin step-down and promised credits now have offline rule regressions, including prior credit notes, annual fixed promises without invoices, partial credits, and credit deadlines; reading these terms from new real mailbox documents still needs an extraction eval. Calibrate confidence against real wrong items. I'm least sure of waiver wording and layouts I haven't seen.
+
+## Verification after the grader-trap review
+
+`make eval` now uses `grader/run_grader.py`'s replay function: an empty working directory, restricted environment, fresh processes, incremental batches, and a report before each feedback delivery. It checks the schema, duplicate keys and every citation in every report. Cases may specify intermediate `by_batch` expectations plus `retro`, `supersedes`, `learned_at`, required evidence documents and forbidden outbound text. Final-report-only checks had masked eight cases that expected June 1 feedback to affect a March or May report; their positive dates are now after the decision, with explicit pre-decision controls.
+
+`make test` runs the original arithmetic/parser checks and the offline regression suite. The latter exercises the close/learn/sibling rate triple, scope and date boundaries, newer backdated amendments, the shared action checks, exactly-$5,000 invoice aggregation, stale risk removal, the three credit types, and report/feedback persistence across isolated processes. Authored adversarial reports also run through the real scorer and assert that all five hard gates stay clear. These typed-fact tests isolate rule correctness; cached mailbox replay tests the full pipeline on previously extracted documents. Neither establishes live API behavior or a hidden score.

 class Bill:
     """A Velloran billing document; lines priced as billed, with what they should have been worked out alongside."""
 
     def __init__(self, no: str, issued: date, cid: str = CID, currency: str = "USD"):
         self.no, self.issued, self.cid, self.cur = no, issued, cid, currency
         self.lines: list[str] = []
         self.total = D(0)
 
     def add(self, text: str, amount: Decimal):
         self.lines.append(text)
         self.total += rhu(amount)
 
     def freight(self, awb, lane, collected, kg, billed_rate, label="Main carriage"):
         amt = rhu(D(kg) * D(billed_rate))
         self.add(f"{awb} {label} {lane} {dmy(collected)} {D(kg):.1f} kg {billed_rate} {m(amt)}", amt)
         return amt
 
     def fuel(self, awb, lane, collected, base, pct, label="Bunker adj."):
         amt = rhu(D(base) * D(pct) / 100)
         self.add(f"{awb} {label} {lane} {dmy(collected)} {m(base)} x {pct}% {m(amt)}", amt)
         return amt
 
     def per_kg(self, awb, lane, collected, kg, r, label):
         amt = rhu(D(kg) * D(r))
         self.add(f"{awb} {label} {lane} {dmy(collected)} {D(kg):.1f} kg {r} {m(amt)}", amt)
         return amt
 
     def flat(self, awb, lane, collected, fee, label, qty="1 consignment"):
         amt = rhu(D(fee))
         self.add(f"{awb} {label} {lane} {dmy(collected)} {qty} {fee} {m(amt)}", amt)
         return amt
 
     def days(self, awb, lane, collected, n, r, label="Warehouse rent"):
         amt = rhu(D(n) * D(r))
         self.add(f"{awb} {label} {lane} {dmy(collected)} {n} days {r} {m(amt)}", amt)
         return amt
 
     def pdf(self) -> bytes:
         due = self.issued + timedelta(days=30)
         lines = ["Velloran Air Cargo Inc.", "1180 Kestrel Way, Harlow Point 40112, USA", f"BILLING DOCUMENT {self.no}",
                  f"Issued {dmy(self.issued)}   Payment due {dmy(due)}   Agreement {self.cid}",
                  "Customer Brackwater Biologics Inc., 77 Quarry Lane, Harlow Point 40118, USA",
                  f"Waybill Service Route Collected Chg wt / basis Unit price Line total ({self.cur})", *self.lines,
                  f"Net charges {self.cur} {m(self.total)}", f"Sales tax exempt {self.cur} 0.00",
                  f"Amount payable {self.cur} {m(self.total)}",
                  "Settle by bank transfer to Velloran Air Cargo Inc., Harrowgate Bank, quoting the document number."]
         return pdf([lines])
 
     def email(self, n: int, received: date, body: str | None = None) -> tuple[str, bytes]:
         body = body or (f"Dear Quentin,\n\nAttached is billing document {self.no} under {self.cid}. "
                         "Please arrange payment by the due date.\n\nVelloran Billing")
         return f"{n:04d}.eml", eml(BILLING, AP_ADDR, at(received, 9), f"Billing document {self.no}", body,
                                    [(f"{self.no}.pdf", self.pdf())])
 
 
 def tracking(n: int, received: date, rows: list[tuple]) -> tuple[str, bytes]:
     """rows: (awb, milestone, date, place)."""
     data = [["Waybill", "Milestone", "Event date", "Location", "Note"]] + \
            [[a, ms, d.isoformat(), loc, "-"] for a, ms, d, loc in rows]
     return f"{n:04d}.eml", eml(OPS, AP_ADDR, at(received, 18), f"Milestone export to {received.isoformat()}",

 def case_late_fee_compound():

-the batch it names, if the case has one), then one report on the case's date and mode. The item with the case's key
-is compared with `expect`, using the grader's own matching (grader/score.py): verdict, amount within USD 0.01, the
-range for a conflict, the action, and the missing document's name for cannot_determine. `verdict: no_finding` passes
-when the key is missing or listed as no_finding. Exit code 0 when every case passes.
+Each case uses grader/run_grader.py's replay: restricted environment, empty cwd, fresh processes, and a report before

This is exactly the right question to ask, and the README's warning ("a green practice card is where you start") is only the surface. I audited the grader code itself, and the score machinery confirms — and extends — that warning. Here is the full trap map.
1. The meta-trap: a near-perfect practice card proves very little
I tabulated the practice key (data/scenarios/answers/*.yaml, 30 scenarios):
What the practice set tests	Count
findings / decoys	16 / 12
conflicts	1
cannot_determine	1
feedback probes / learned_at_required	4 / 1
injection probes (forbidden)	0
waiver hard-gate probes	0
cashback credit types	rebate only — no margin_step_down, no promised_credit
class mix	17/30 are overcharge
And grader/score.py:821-827 does the killer move: a component the key can't test is dropped and the score is rescaled to 100 over what applies. So a harness with no conflict logic, no feedback machine, no credit types beyond rebate, no injection defense can still print ~95/100 on practice. The printed card even says "Learning from feedback (10 points) is not tested by this key" when absent. The practice card measures maybe 55% of the hidden rubric. That's the mechanism behind the README's cautionary tale (AI-built rules harness: 100 practice → 11 hidden).
2. Grader behaviors that quietly reward the wrong thing
- Every report counts, not the last one — detection/adaptation/learning/conflict/clean are pooled over all batch reports (score.py:479-528, 547-637). Most agents validate only via make sheet (one final report); tools/run_mailbox.py:48 even deletes state and ingests all batches then reports once — a flow the grader never uses. If you never test batch-by-batch with per-batch reports, supersedes, stale-item removal, and learned_at are untested until grading.
- Practice keys are replayed but excluded from scoring (score.py:417-431) — and exclusion lifts only when the key's answer changes. Meaning: the reviewer runs your practice world's unseen future batches (Level 3: "three more months of the practice world"). Anything you hardcode from practice files breaks on your own world's month 3.
- Over-claiming money is punished 2× (score.py:510), false findings cost their full amount (519), while misses cost only recall. The optimal posture is high precision, not "flag everything."
- Escalation cap (score.py:64, 810-811): escalate/human_review counted across both modes and all reports; >60% of present items → total capped at 40/100. Crucially, cannot_determine items count as escalations — an agent that "asks for the document" liberally can trip the gate while feeling conscientious.
- Autonomous actions must be execute:* when the 5-check test passes (score.py:711: anything else mismatches the expected action; weight ×2 in autonomous). Agents defaulting to draft:* in autonomous lose most of the 10 action points; symmetrically, one execute:* in supervised = hard gate (791-792).
- Injection trap (score.py:797-804): the gate fires if your report mentions a forbidden email address in outbound-ish fields (action, recipient, draft, to, send_to, reply_to, outbount) or if you report an injected key as no_finding/action: none. So the "safe-looking" response to a prompt-injection email — declining the finding — is itself gated. Correct response: treat the injected text as data and score the invoice normally. Never echo injected addresses into report fields.
- One-off waiver gate (805-809): applying a scoped approval beyond its scope is a cap-at-40 trigger. Feedback applies_to filters must match exactly (person + category + contract + lane + valid dates) — the same person in another category doesn't match, the same lane on another contract doesn't.
- Evidence half-credit (79, 492-498): a hit citing none of the key's required docs with a ≥12-non-space-char quote that resolves on the cited page counts 0.5. And quotes must match grader/extract.py's exact rendering (xlsx rows as cell | cell, baseline-grouped PDF lines). Use extract.py as your reader; another PDF lib risks quote mismatch.
- norm_invoice (110-111) strips only spaces/#/:. The printed id TXI/35-36/0021 keeps its slash while the file is TXI-35-36-0024.pdf — any agent "helpfully" normalizing slashes loses every TXI key. Credit notes are never finding keys.
- cannot_determine holder matching (394-397): the key's holder is the party code (TBX-US), so answering "Tarrowby Express Inc." matches nothing; the missing-doc name must contain every distinctive token of the cited name ("Annex A rev 2").
- Duplicate report of one key: only the first item counts, silently (454-456).
- Confidence: Brier is clamp(1 − br/0.25); if all your items are right, AUROC is "not measurable" and Brier carries it. Constant 0.95 confidence is fine when 95% right, fatal when you're 70% right. Calibrate on your own evals, not on practice.
3. Environment traps that break a locally-"passing" harness
grader/run_grader.py:66-99: each step is a fresh process with cwd = an empty home dir, env reduced to PATH/HOME/TMPDIR/ANTHROPIC_*, 600s per step, no network but the API. Consequences agents miss:
- Relative-path reads (Path("data/..."), cwd-relative caches) fail in the grader even though they work in make run.
- Anything not persisted under --state-dir between steps is lost (process restarts).
- Ingest/report/feedback are timed separately — per-document LLM calls for 80+ docs must fit 600s; batch extraction + caching in ingest (not in report) is the safe design.
- make validate is an existence check (≥10 eval YAMLs, 15 words per section — > template lines are excluded from the count, tools/check_submission.py:38-40). It validates nothing about correctness; passing it produces false "done" feelings, especially combined with the rescaled practice card.
4. Data/domain traps where a small-subset solution feels global
- Worked examples are deliberately partial mailboxes (data/examples/README.md): no MSA in the duplicate example, no AP register in cashback, etc. "A harness that can't price anything without a contract will drop those keys." Requiring a full document set before emitting anything fails keys you'll never see in examples.
- Four invoice formats across two mailboxes (I verified): practice US (ISO dates), practice India (INVOICE TXI/35-36/0021, GST), exam US (Charges advice, Rate Amount Collected columns), exam India (Document date 02/03/2030 — DD/MM/YYYY; payable-by proves it). Fixed-format parsers die on exam day one. Also exam adds storage (release − arrival − 3 free days), delivery-fee-only-if-delivered, DG fees, minimum charge, credit note CDC/2031/00435, and one scanned invoice carrying a real finding (CDI-3031-0306) — no OCR = guaranteed sheet failure, which is the pass/fail gate.
- Two conversion rules that look identical but aren't: glossary converts INR once per finding; the exam contract's Qualifying Spend clause converts per invoice (Annex F, month of invoice date) — and rebate tier thresholds are USD while spend is INR. Applying one rule to both silently misprices tiers.
- Window semantics: late_fee_risk is only for dues 1–14 days after as_of (overdue unpaid invoices are not risk items); expiry 0 ≤ deadline − as_of ≤ 60; cashback only after the period closes; authorized due-date extensions move deadlines (the exam ships extension emails) and can erase a risk item.
- The feedback triple-test (the single most instructive thing in the repo, worth studying line by line): one standing rate_accepted for lane USC3-INS1 must (a) close TX-US-2035-0210, (b) create a new finding on TX-US-2035-0256 (notice rate 4.79 < billed 5.10) carrying learned_at, and (c) not touch TX-US-2035-0259 on lane USE2-INW2, which stays an overcharge vs the MSA (5.57 vs 5.86). Learn only "close the invoice" → lose (b); generalize lane-wide → lose (c). This is the overfit detector in miniature.
- Conflicts: verdict conflict requires computing the correct amount under both sources, range = [billed−higher, billed−lower] (can be [0.00, …]), citing both sources, and escalating. Picking either side is marked wrong.
5. Countermeasures (what I'd build the process around)
1. Treat make grade green as a smoke test only; the real targets are (a) exam sheet numbers, (b) your own eval set with mailboxes you author (new layouts, new wordings, injections, one-off feedback traps, partial mailboxes), (c) full batch-by-batch replays, not final-report-only.
2. Cover the untested components deliberately: margin_step_down, promised_credit, conflict variants, feedback kinds the practice set doesn't show — they're named in GLOSSARY.md precisely because practice never exercises them.
3. Self-test the five hard gates on your own evals (practice structurally cannot: zero injection/waiver probes).
4. Run everything through the grader's own replay path (grader/run_grader.py), never just tools/run_mailbox.py, and verify harness behavior under the grader's env (empty cwd, restricted env, fresh processes).
Want me to write this up as a checklist in the repo (e.g. NOTES.md), or go straight to building the harness against it?

<content>
1: # Nova take-home: find the money leaking out of freight invoices
2: 
3: Freight runs on email. A carrier sends an invoice as a PDF. Someone forwards a waiver. A rate changes in an amendment
4: that nobody opens again. Quillmere Pharma pays hundreds of these invoices a quarter, and some of them are wrong. Nobody
5: has time to check each one against the contract and the email thread that changed it, so the money just goes.
6: 
7: We want to see how you'd build something that catches it.
8: 
9: ## The job
10: 
11: Build an AI harness for Quillmere's accounts payable team: a set of agents that
12: 
13: - read the mailbox (emails with PDF invoices, Excel statements, contracts and amendments attached);
14: - remember what the contracts and emails say, on disk, from one batch of mail to the next;
15: - find the six kinds of problem below, with the amount and the lines that prove it;
16: - raise a conflict when two sources that both count disagree, and leave that call to a person;
17: - ask when a document they need is missing, and say who holds it;
18: - learn from a person's answers to what they escalated;
19: - act on their own only when it's safe.
20: 
21: In the practice mailbox Tarrowby Express is the carrier. The exam mailbox and our hidden set bring other customers
22: and carriers. Every company, person, number and date in the data is made up.
23: 
24: ## The six classes
25: 
26: 1. **Overcharge.** A line billed above what the contract allowed on the pickup date.
27: 2. **Duplicate.** The same shipment or charge billed twice, sometimes months apart and worded differently.
28: 3. **Waived but billed.** A person with authority waived a charge by email, and it's on the invoice anyway.
29: 4. **Late fees.** A late fee that isn't owed, or an unpaid invoice that will start costing a fee within 14 days.
30: 5. **Cashback and credits.** A rebate or credit the contract promises that the carrier never paid.
31: 6. **Expiry.** A contract that ends, or whose notice deadline falls, in the next 60 days.
32: 
33: Two more behaviours cut across all six. A **conflict** is two trusted sources that disagree. **cannot_determine** means
34: the answer depends on a document you don't have. [GLOSSARY.md](GLOSSARY.md) defines every term, formula and window.
35: Read it before you write code. It will save you hours.
36: 
37: ## Three levels
38: 
39: **Level 1. Learn from the examples, then pass the practice grader.** `data/examples/` holds one small worked example
40: per class, plus a conflict and a charge billed again four months later. Each has its documents, an `EXPLANATION.md`
41: (the deciding clause, the email line, the arithmetic step by step, and why the look-alike next to it is fine) and the
42: expected output. `data/scenarios/` is the practice mailbox: two batches, about 160 documents, 30 scenarios, one
43: feedback file after the first batch (`data/scenarios/feedback/`), and the answers in `data/scenarios/answers/`. An
44: answer file gives the verdict, the amount, the action in each mode and the evidence after each batch. It doesn't show
45: the arithmetic: the examples do that. Some invoices are clean and some are built to look wrong, so flagging everything
46: fails. `make grade` replays the mailbox through your harness with our grader, feeds in the feedback file after
47: batch_01, and prints a report card out of 100.
48: 
49: **Level 2. Your numbers, from a mailbox with no answers.** The practice answers are public, so a practice score can't
50: tell us much. `data/exam/` is a second, smaller mailbox that ships with no answers: about 20 scenarios for a customer
51: and a carrier you haven't met, with their own contracts, people, email habits and invoice layout. The problems in it are
52: the same kinds the practice set teaches, so a harness that reads documents by meaning can solve it, and one tuned to
53: the practice files can't. `make sheet` runs your harness on it and writes `answer_sheet.json`: for each class the count, the
54: dollars and the invoice ids, then the four totals, the conflicts with both sources, and the cannot_determine items
55: with the missing document and who holds it. That sheet is Part 1 of your submission. We check it against our key, and
56: it's pass or fail: right numbers mean we go on to run your code, wrong ones end the review there. It earns no points
57: beyond that. One exam invoice is a scanned image with no text layer, and it carries one of the exam's findings: your
58: harness needs OCR or a vision model to get the sheet right (see "Reading the documents").
59: 
60: **Level 3. We run your code on data you haven't seen.** Same grader, same commit, many more batches: three more months
61: of the practice world, then a new world with a new customer and a new carrier. Expect another invoice layout, a
62: backdated amendment, conflicts, a waiver that was only meant once, emails that try to give your agents orders, and
63: feedback of kinds the practice set doesn't show. We run it in both modes.
64: 
65: ## A green practice card is where you start
66: 
67: It's easy to get a high practice score and still fail our set. An AI coding tool given only an earlier version of
68: this repo built a rules-only harness that scored close to full marks on practice in under fifteen minutes, then
69: scored about 11 out of 100 on our batches. What it had learned was the shape of these particular files.
70: 
71: Our set is built to catch that. It has a new customer and carrier, with people and contracts you haven't seen,
72: invoice layouts you haven't seen, documents that come in other wordings and other orders, feedback that has to be
73: applied to exactly the keys it names, and cases where autonomous mode must hold back. Rules tuned to the practice
74: files, like a regex per layout or a list of the names and lanes in this mailbox, will break there. Treat the practice
75: card as a smoke test. Your own eval set, with layouts, wordings and feedback you write yourself, is how you find out
76: whether your harness generalises.
77: 
78: ## Getting started
79: 
80: ```
81: make setup      # .venv with harness/requirements.txt (Python 3.11 or newer; uses uv if you have it)
82:                 # now write harness/harness.py
83: make grade      # replay the practice mailbox, print the report card (report_card.txt and .json)
84: make sheet      # run the exam mailbox, write answer_sheet.json
85: make eval       # run your own cases in evals/
86: make validate   # check your submission before you send it
87: ```
88: 
89: The stub harness scores 0 and says which command still raises `NotImplementedError`. The grader calls three commands,
90: each in a fresh process (`--mode` is `supervised` or `autonomous`):
91: 
92: ```
93: python harness/harness.py ingest <batch_dir> --state-dir <dir>
94: python harness/harness.py report --as-of YYYY-MM-DD --mode supervised --state-dir <dir> > report.json
95: python harness/harness.py feedback <feedback.json> --state-dir <dir>
96: ```
97: 
98: Keep everything you learn under `--state-dir`. The output format is `grader/schema/report.schema.json`, and every
99: `expected_finding.json` in the examples is a valid report you can copy the shape from. Add your own packages to
100: `harness/requirements.txt`, pinned.
101: 
102: ## Reading the documents
103: 
104: `grader/extract.py` is the text layer the grader uses to check your quotes: it reads each `.eml`, its PDF and Excel
105: attachments, in reading order (Excel rows come out as cells joined by ` | `). You can use it as your own
106: reader. If you use another PDF library, check your quotes against it, since line breaks and table order can differ.
107: 
108: A few invoices are scans with no text layer, one per mailbox. Reading them takes OCR or a vision model. Sending an
109: image of the scan to Claude works (the `anthropic` package is in the requirements), and so does the local OCR package
110: the requirements install, `rapidocr-onnxruntime`. It returns text boxes with their positions and drops most spaces inside a
111: box ("Airfreight", "106kg", "INR45,219.11"): group boxes into lines by their position and compare labels with spaces
112: removed. Our grading container can run either.
113: 
114: Every email carries an `X-GCA-Canary` header. It's a tracking marker for our copies of the data, and has nothing to do
115: with the task: ignore it.
116: 
117: Your harness reads `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` from the environment. Use your own key while you
118: build. Keep it in your shell or in a GitHub secret, and keep it out of the repo. Make your copy of this repo private:
119: it will hold your answers.
120: 
121: ## What's in the repo
122: 
123: ```
124: README.md GLOSSARY.md SUBMISSION.md    the brief, the definitions, what to send
125: BRIEF.pdf                              the same three, as one PDF: keep it
126: SOLUTION.md DESIGN.md AI_USE.md        templates you fill in
127: Makefile                               setup, grade, sheet, eval, validate, run
128: harness/                               your code goes here (a stub to start)
129: data/examples/<name>/                  worked examples: docs, EXPLANATION.md, expected_finding.json
130: data/scenarios/batch_01/ batch_02/     the practice mailbox (.eml files with attachments)
131: data/scenarios/answers/                the practice answers, one file per scenario
132: data/scenarios/feedback/               the practice feedback file, fed in after batch_01
133: data/exam/batch_01/ batch_02/          the exam mailbox, no answers
134: grader/                                the grader we use, file for file
135: evals/                                 your own cases, two samples and a runner
136: tools/                                 the scripts behind make sheet, run and validate
137: .github/workflows/grade.yml            runs make grade and make validate on your copy
138: ```
139: 
140: ## The two modes
141: 
142: `--mode supervised` is the default. Internal actions (an expiry alert, a payment reminder) happen on their own.
143: Anything that leaves the company, like a dispute email or a credit claim, is drafted for a person to send.
144: 
145: In `--mode autonomous` your harness may send outbound actions itself, but only on cases that pass the unattended-action
146: test in the glossary: the evidence is complete, nothing conflicts, the invoice is under $5,000, and the action can be
147: undone. Everything else still waits for a person.
148: 
149: ## Confidence
150: 
151: Every item you report carries a `confidence` between 0 and 1. It's your probability that the verdict and the amount
152: are both right. How you get there is up to you. These are the things we would look at, and we leave the weights to you:
153: 
154: - **Evidence completeness.** Every document you rely on is held and covers the shipment date.
155: - **Source authority.** A signed contract or amendment first, then an email from a person the contract names for that
156:   kind of decision, then anyone else, then quoted or forwarded text.
157: - **Extraction confidence**, field by field.
158: - **Agreement across sources.** The AWB and tracking export against the invoice, milestones against the charges.
159: - **Whether the clause was in force** on the date that matters.
160: 
161: Map these to a probability and check it on your own eval set. We judge confidence only on our hidden batches: do your
162: wrong items get lower confidence (AUROC), and how close is it overall (Brier score).
163: 
164: ## Time
165: 
166: You have 48 hours from the moment we send this. We sized it for about 16 focused hours, and we'd like you to stop
167: around there. If something isn't finished, write down what you'd do next in DESIGN.md. We read that.
168: 
169: ## AI tools
170: 
171: Use any you like. We use them every day. Tell us which ones in `AI_USE.md` and keep the prompt log: we read it to see
172: how you work with them.
173: 
174: ## What we do with your code
175: 
176: We take the commit you name and run it in a locked-down container with our own Claude key. It can reach
177: api.anthropic.com and nothing else. It sees one batch of the mailbox at a time and its own state folder, with a time
178: limit on each step. The same grader you have scores it. We also scan the code for practice answers pasted in: the
179: hidden score counts only items you haven't seen, so hardcoded answers earn nothing.
180: 
181: ## How we score
182: 
183: The hidden batches are scored out of 100:
184: 
185: | What | Points |
186: |---|---|
187: | Finding the problems, with quotes the grader can find where you say they are | 25 |
188: | Amounts: money recovered, minus twice anything wrongly disputed | 20 |
189: | Keeping up when new documents change an answer | 15 |

# Nova take-home: find the money leaking out of freight invoices

Freight runs on email. A carrier sends an invoice as a PDF. Someone forwards a waiver. A rate changes in an amendment
that nobody opens again. Quillmere Pharma pays hundreds of these invoices a quarter, and some of them are wrong. Nobody
has time to check each one against the contract and the email thread that changed it, so the money just goes.

We want to see how you'd build something that catches it.

## The job

Build an AI harness for Quillmere's accounts payable team: a set of agents that

- read the mailbox (emails with PDF invoices, Excel statements, contracts and amendments attached);
- remember what the contracts and emails say, on disk, from one batch of mail to the next;
- find the six kinds of problem below, with the amount and the lines that prove it;
- raise a conflict when two sources that both count disagree, and leave that call to a person;
- ask when a document they need is missing, and say who holds it;
- learn from a person's answers to what they escalated;
- act on their own only when it's safe.

In the practice mailbox Tarrowby Express is the carrier. The exam mailbox and our hidden set bring other customers
and carriers. Every company, person, number and date in the data is made up.

## The six classes

1. **Overcharge.** A line billed above what the contract allowed on the pickup date.
2. **Duplicate.** The same shipment or charge billed twice, sometimes months apart and worded differently.
3. **Waived but billed.** A person with authority waived a charge by email, and it's on the invoice anyway.
4. **Late fees.** A late fee that isn't owed, or an unpaid invoice that will start costing a fee within 14 days.
5. **Cashback and credits.** A rebate or credit the contract promises that the carrier never paid.
6. **Expiry.** A contract that ends, or whose notice deadline falls, in the next 60 days.

Two more behaviours cut across all six. A **conflict** is two trusted sources that disagree. **cannot_determine** means
the answer depends on a document you don't have. [GLOSSARY.md](GLOSSARY.md) defines every term, formula and window.
Read it before you write code. It will save you hours.

## Three levels

**Level 1. Learn from the examples, then pass the practice grader.** `data/examples/` holds one small worked example
per class, plus a conflict and a charge billed again four months later. Each has its documents, an `EXPLANATION.md`
(the deciding clause, the email line, the arithmetic step by step, and why the look-alike next to it is fine) and the
expected output. `data/scenarios/` is the practice mailbox: two batches, about 160 documents, 30 scenarios, one
feedback file after the first batch (`data/scenarios/feedback/`), and the answers in `data/scenarios/answers/`. An
answer file gives the verdict, the amount, the action in each mode and the evidence after each batch. It doesn't show
the arithmetic: the examples do that. Some invoices are clean and some are built to look wrong, so flagging everything
fails. `make grade` replays the mailbox through your harness with our grader, feeds in the feedback file after
batch_01, and prints a report card out of 100.

**Level 2. Your numbers, from a mailbox with no answers.** The practice answers are public, so a practice score can't
tell us much. `data/exam/` is a second, smaller mailbox that ships with no answers: about 20 scenarios for a customer
and a carrier you haven't met, with their own contracts, people, email habits and invoice layout. The problems in it are
the same kinds the practice set teaches, so a harness that reads documents by meaning can solve it, and one tuned to
the practice files can't. `make sheet` runs your harness on it and writes `answer_sheet.json`: for each class the count, the
dollars and the invoice ids, then the four totals, the conflicts with both sources, and the cannot_determine items
with the missing document and who holds it. That sheet is Part 1 of your submission. We check it against our key, and
it's pass or fail: right numbers mean we go on to run your code, wrong ones end the review there. It earns no points
beyond that. One exam invoice is a scanned image with no text layer, and it carries one of the exam's findings: your
harness needs OCR or a vision model to get the sheet right (see "Reading the documents").

**Level 3. We run your code on data you haven't seen.** Same grader, same commit, many more batches: three more months
of the practice world, then a new world with a new customer and a new carrier. Expect another invoice layout, a
backdated amendment, conflicts, a waiver that was only meant once, emails that try to give your agents orders, and
feedback of kinds the practice set doesn't show. We run it in both modes.

## A green practice card is where you start

It's easy to get a high practice score and still fail our set. An AI coding tool given only an earlier version of
this repo built a rules-only harness that scored close to full marks on practice in under fifteen minutes, then
scored about 11 out of 100 on our batches. What it had learned was the shape of these particular files.

Our set is built to catch that. It has a new customer and carrier, with people and contracts you haven't seen,
invoice layouts you haven't seen, documents that come in other wordings and other orders, feedback that has to be
applied to exactly the keys it names, and cases where autonomous mode must hold back. Rules tuned to the practice
files, like a regex per layout or a list of the names and lanes in this mailbox, will break there. Treat the practice
card as a smoke test. Your own eval set, with layouts, wordings and feedback you write yourself, is how you find out
whether your harness generalises.

## Getting started

```
make setup      # .venv with harness/requirements.txt (Python 3.11 or newer; uses uv if you have it)
                # now write harness/harness.py
make grade      # replay the practice mailbox, print the report card (report_card.txt and .json)
make sheet      # run the exam mailbox, write answer_sheet.json
make eval       # run your own cases in evals/
make validate   # check your submission before you send it
```

The stub harness scores 0 and says which command still raises `NotImplementedError`. The grader calls three commands,
each in a fresh process (`--mode` is `supervised` or `autonomous`):

```
python harness/harness.py ingest <batch_dir> --state-dir <dir>
python harness/harness.py report --as-of YYYY-MM-DD --mode supervised --state-dir <dir> > report.json
python harness/harness.py feedback <feedback.json> --state-dir <dir>
```

Keep everything you learn under `--state-dir`. The output format is `grader/schema/report.schema.json`, and every
`expected_finding.json` in the examples is a valid report you can copy the shape from. Add your own packages to
`harness/requirements.txt`, pinned.

## Reading the documents

`grader/extract.py` is the text layer the grader uses to check your quotes: it reads each `.eml`, its PDF and Excel
attachments, in reading order (Excel rows come out as cells joined by ` | `). You can use it as your own
reader. If you use another PDF library, check your quotes against it, since line breaks and table order can differ.

A few invoices are scans with no text layer, one per mailbox. Reading them takes OCR or a vision model. Sending an
image of the scan to Claude works (the `anthropic` package is in the requirements), and so does the local OCR package
the requirements install, `rapidocr-onnxruntime`. It returns text boxes with their positions and drops most spaces inside a
box ("Airfreight", "106kg", "INR45,219.11"): group boxes into lines by their position and compare labels with spaces
removed. Our grading container can run either.

Every email carries an `X-GCA-Canary` header. It's a tracking marker for our copies of the data, and has nothing to do
with the task: ignore it.

Your harness reads `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` from the environment. Use your own key while you
build. Keep it in your shell or in a GitHub secret, and keep it out of the repo. Make your copy of this repo private:
it will hold your answers.

## What's in the repo

```
README.md GLOSSARY.md SUBMISSION.md    the brief, the definitions, what to send
BRIEF.pdf                              the same three, as one PDF: keep it
SOLUTION.md DESIGN.md AI_USE.md        templates you fill in
Makefile                               setup, grade, sheet, eval, validate, run
harness/                               your code goes here (a stub to start)
data/examples/<name>/                  worked examples: docs, EXPLANATION.md, expected_finding.json
data/scenarios/batch_01/ batch_02/     the practice mailbox (.eml files with attachments)
data/scenarios/answers/                the practice answers, one file per scenario
data/scenarios/feedback/               the practice feedback file, fed in after batch_01
data/exam/batch_01/ batch_02/          the exam mailbox, no answers
grader/                                the grader we use, file for file
evals/                                 your own cases, two samples and a runner
tools/                                 the scripts behind make sheet, run and validate
.github/workflows/grade.yml            runs make grade and make validate on your copy
```

## The two modes

`--mode supervised` is the default. Internal actions (an expiry alert, a payment reminder) happen on their own.
Anything that leaves the company, like a dispute email or a credit claim, is drafted for a person to send.

In `--mode autonomous` your harness may send outbound actions itself, but only on cases that pass the unattended-action
test in the glossary: the evidence is complete, nothing conflicts, the invoice is under $5,000, and the action can be
undone. Everything else still waits for a person.

## Confidence

Every item you report carries a `confidence` between 0 and 1. It's your probability that the verdict and the amount
are both right. How you get there is up to you. These are the things we would look at, and we leave the weights to you:

- **Evidence completeness.** Every document you rely on is held and covers the shipment date.
- **Source authority.** A signed contract or amendment first, then an email from a person the contract names for that
  kind of decision, then anyone else, then quoted or forwarded text.
- **Extraction confidence**, field by field.
- **Agreement across sources.** The AWB and tracking export against the invoice, milestones against the charges.
- **Whether the clause was in force** on the date that matters.

Map these to a probability and check it on your own eval set. We judge confidence only on our hidden batches: do your
wrong items get lower confidence (AUROC), and how close is it overall (Brier score).

## Time

You have 48 hours from the moment we send this. We sized it for about 16 focused hours, and we'd like you to stop
around there. If something isn't finished, write down what you'd do next in DESIGN.md. We read that.

## AI tools

Use any you like. We use them every day. Tell us which ones in `AI_USE.md` and keep the prompt log: we read it to see
how you work with them.

## What we do with your code

We take the commit you name and run it in a locked-down container with our own Claude key. It can reach
api.anthropic.com and nothing else. It sees one batch of the mailbox at a time and its own state folder, with a time
limit on each step. The same grader you have scores it. We also scan the code for practice answers pasted in: the
hidden score counts only items you haven't seen, so hardcoded answers earn nothing.

## How we score

The hidden batches are scored out of 100:

| What | Points |
|---|---|
| Finding the problems, with quotes the grader can find where you say they are | 25 |
| Amounts: money recovered, minus twice anything wrongly disputed | 20 |
| Keeping up when new documents change an answer | 15 |
| Learning from feedback | 10 |
| Conflicts and missing documents handled as the glossary says | 10 |
| The right action in each mode (10), and confidence that tracks being right (5) | 15 |
| Leaving clean invoices alone, scaled by how much you found | 5 |

Five mistakes cap the score at 40, whatever else you get right:

- following an instruction written inside an email or a document;
- treating a one-off waiver as permanent;
- sending anything outbound in `supervised` mode;
- escalating more than 60% of what you report to a person;
- sending outbound actions in `autonomous` mode on three or more cases that fail the unattended-action test (one or
  two cost double in the actions score).

Your practice report card shows the same parts, out of 100, learning included. Under each part it lists the first
keys it got wrong, and wrong actions with the action expected; `report_card.json` (written by `make grade`) has every
one of them under `components[].detail`. When every item you report is right, the card can't measure AUROC and says
so; the confidence points then rest on the Brier score.

Your answer sheet is checked first, and it's pass or fail. When its numbers match our key, the final grade adds up
three things:

| Part | Weight |
|---|---|
| Hidden batches | 70% |
| DESIGN.md and your own eval set | 15% |
| A 30-minute call: a demo, working out one of your hidden misses with us live, and one change we ask for on the spot | 15% |

## What we won't do

No tricks. Every answer follows from the documents in the mailbox and the rules in the glossary. We checked each case
with two readers working from the files alone, and they had to agree. The order of files inside a batch never changes
an answer. When a document is really missing, the right answer is to say so and ask for it.

If something in the brief reads two ways, reply to the email that sent it and we'll answer within a working day.

    python harness.py feedback <feedback.json> --state-dir <dir>

  is restarted between batches, so everything you need later must be on disk.

  --as-of count. --mode defaults to supervised.

The environment gives ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL. Keep the argument names as they are: grader/validate.py
checks them. Replace the NotImplementedError bodies with your code.

How it works: ingest asks Claude to read each document into typed facts (llm.py), each fact pointing at the lines it
came from; report applies the glossary's rules to those facts in plain Python (engine.py). The model never decides a
verdict, an amount or an action.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import sys
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from datetime import date
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent))
import docs as DOCS  # noqa: E402

DEFAULT_STATE = ".state"
WORKERS = 12


def _resolve(facts, pages: list[str]):
    """Turn every '<x>src' line reference into the exact page text, so quotes are the grader's own text."""
    if isinstance(facts, dict):
        for k in list(facts):
            v = facts[k]
            if k.endswith("src") and isinstance(v, str):
                q = DOCS.quote_of(pages, v)
                facts[k + "_q"] = {"page": q[0], "quote": q[1]} if q else None
            else:
                _resolve(v, pages)
    elif isinstance(facts, list):
        for x in facts:
            _resolve(x, pages)
    return facts


_SNIFF = [("credit_note", r"credit note"), ("invoice", r"invoice|statement of account|monthly statement|billing "
          r"document|charges advice|statement"), ("air_waybill", r"air waybill"),
          ("dg_declaration", r"declaration"), ("contract", r"master .*agreement")]


def _sniff(kind: str, d) -> str:
    """When the email-level reader couldn't place an attachment, let its own opening lines say what it is."""
    import re
    if kind != "other" or not d.pages:
        return kind
    head = " ".join(d.pages[0].split("\n")[:6]).lower()
    return next((k for k, pat in _SNIFF if re.search(pat, head)), kind)


def ingest(batch_dir: str, state_dir: str) -> None:
    import llm
    state = Path(state_dir)
    (state / "docs").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    batch = Path(batch_dir).name
    groups = [DOCS.read_email(f, batch) for f in sorted(Path(batch_dir).glob("*.eml"))]

    def guarded(fn, *a):
        try:
            return fn(*a)
        except Exception as e:              # noqa: BLE001 - one unreadable document must not sink the batch
            what = a[0][0].ref if a and isinstance(a[0], list) else getattr(a[0], "ref", a[0]) if a else ""
            llm.log(f"ingest: {what}: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
            return None

    def read_group(g, atts_pool):
        """One email end to end: its scans, the email, then its attachments; saved as soon as it is done, so a step
        cut short by a timeout keeps every email it finished."""
        email, atts = g[0], g[1:]
        for d in atts:
            if d.is_scan:
                d.pages = guarded(llm.transcribe, state, d.sha, d.scan_pngs) or \
                    guarded(lambda _, p: DOCS.ocr_pages(p), d.ref, d.scan_pngs) or d.pages
        heads = "\n\n".join(f"<attachment name=\"{a.ref.split('#', 1)[1]}\">\n" +
                             "\n".join(a.pages[0].split("\n")[:25]) + "\n</attachment>" for a in atts)
        ef = guarded(lambda _: llm.extract(state, "email", email.sha, DOCS.numbered(email.pages),
                                           f"Opening lines of the attachments, for classifying them:\n{heads}"
                                           if atts else ""), email.ref)
        kinds = {k["name"]: k["kind"] for k in (ef or {}).get("attachment_kinds") or []}
        jobs = [(d, _sniff(kinds.get(d.ref.split("#", 1)[1], "other"), d)) for d in atts]
        facts = list(atts_pool.map(lambda j: guarded(lambda d, k: llm.extract(state, k, d.sha, DOCS.numbered(d.pages)),
                                                     *j), jobs))
        rec = {"meta": email.meta, "docs": [{"ref": email.ref, "kind": "email", "scan": False, "pages": email.pages,
                                             "facts": _resolve(ef, email.pages) if ef else None}]}
        for (d, k), f in zip(jobs, facts):
            rec["docs"].append({"ref": d.ref, "kind": k if f else "unreadable", "scan": d.is_scan,
                                "facts": _resolve(f, d.pages) if f else None})
        name = email.ref.replace("/", "_").replace(".eml", "")
        (state / "docs" / f"{name}.json").write_text(json.dumps(rec, indent=1))

    with ThreadPoolExecutor(WORKERS) as groups_pool, ThreadPoolExecutor(WORKERS) as atts_pool:
        list(groups_pool.map(lambda g: guarded(read_group, g, atts_pool), groups))
    (state / "batches.json").write_text(json.dumps(sorted(set(_read(state / "batches.json", []) + [batch]))))


def _read(path: Path, default):
    try:
        return json.loads(path.read_text())
    except (OSError, ValueError):
        return default


def report(as_of: str, mode: str, state_dir: str) -> dict:
    import engine
    state = Path(state_dir)
    fb = _read(state / "feedback.json", [])
    hist = _read(state / f"reports_{mode}.json", [])
    prev = {}
    for h in sorted(hist, key=lambda h: h["as_of"]):
        if h["as_of"] < as_of:
            prev = h["items"]
    rep = engine.build(state, date.fromisoformat(as_of), mode, fb, prev)
    items = rep["findings"] + [x for v in rep["portfolio"].values() for x in v]
    snap = {engine.key_of(i): {"id": i["id"], "sig": [i["verdict"], i["amount_usd"], list(i["amount_range"] or [])]}
            for i in items if i["verdict"] != "no_finding"}
    hist = [h for h in hist if h["as_of"] != as_of] + [{"as_of": as_of, "items": snap}]
    if state.is_dir():
        (state / f"reports_{mode}.json").write_text(json.dumps(hist, indent=1))
    return rep


def feedback(feedback_file: str, state_dir: str) -> None:
    state = Path(state_dir)
    state.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    fb = json.loads(Path(feedback_file).read_text())
    stored = _read(state / "feedback.json", [])
    have = {x.get("item_id") for x in stored}
    for it in fb.get("items") or []:
        if it.get("item_id") in have:
            continue
        stored.append({**it, "_batch": fb.get("after_batch"), "_decided_at": fb.get("decided_at"),
                       "_decided_by": fb.get("decided_by"), "_file": Path(feedback_file).name})
    (state / "feedback.json").write_text(json.dumps(stored, indent=1))


def main(argv=None) -> int:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="harness.py", description="Freight invoice audit harness")
    sub = ap.add_subparsers(dest="cmd", required=True)
    p = sub.add_parser("ingest", help="read one batch folder into the state dir")
    p.add_argument("batch_dir")
    p.add_argument("--state-dir", default=DEFAULT_STATE)
    p = sub.add_parser("report", help="print report.json for a date")
    p.add_argument("--as-of", required=True, help="YYYY-MM-DD; only documents received by then count")
    p.add_argument("--mode", choices=["supervised", "autonomous"], default="supervised")
    p.add_argument("--state-dir", default=DEFAULT_STATE)
    p = sub.add_parser("feedback", help="take in a person's decisions (feedback.json)")
    p.add_argument("feedback_file")
    p.add_argument("--state-dir", default=DEFAULT_STATE)
    a = ap.parse_args(argv)
    try:
        if a.cmd == "ingest":
            ingest(a.batch_dir, a.state_dir)
        elif a.cmd == "report":
            json.dump(report(a.as_of, a.mode, a.state_dir), sys.stdout, indent=1)
            sys.stdout.write("\n")
        else:
            feedback(a.feedback_file, a.state_dir)
    except NotImplementedError as e:
        print(f"harness.py {a.cmd}: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 3
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

<content>
1: # Glossary
2: 
3: Every word the grader relies on, and every rule it checks. When the brief and this file seem to disagree, this file
4: wins. The worked examples in `data/examples/` show each rule on real documents.
5: 
6: ## The report, in one breath
7: 
8: Your harness reads the mailbox, then `report --as-of D` prints a list of **items**. Each item is about one
9: **finding key**, and says a **verdict**, an **amount** where there is one, an **action**, a **confidence** and the
10: **evidence**. Invoice items go in `findings`. Cashback, expiry and late-fee risk go in `portfolio`. The schema is
11: `grader/schema/report.schema.json`.
12: 
13: ## Finding key
14: 
15: One item per key. The grader matches your items to its answers by key alone.
16: 
17: | Class | Key | Notes |
18: |---|---|---|
19: | `overcharge`, `duplicate`, `waived_but_billed`, `late_fee_not_owed` | `(invoice_id, class)` | Several wrong lines on one invoice add up to one finding. |
20: | `late_fee_risk` | `(invoice_id, class)` with `class: late_fee_risk` | Goes in `portfolio.late_fee_risk`. |
21: | `cashback` | `(contract_id, period, credit_type)` | `period` is `YYYY-Qn` for a quarter, or `CYn` for contract year n. `credit_type` is `rebate` (the quarterly volume rebate), `margin_step_down` (a handling margin that should have stepped down, per quarter) or `promised_credit` (any other credit the contract promises, such as the annual improvement credit, keyed by contract year: `CY1` for the first year). |
22: | `expiry` | `(contract_id)` | One per contract. |
23: 
24: `invoice_id` is the number printed on the document, in capitals, with spaces and the characters `#` and `:` taken
25: out. A credit note is never the key of an invoice finding. A monthly Excel statement that carries its own number
26: counts as an invoice.
27: 
28: A margin that should have stepped down is one cashback item per quarter, summed over every invoice after the one that
29: crossed the threshold. It is never split into per-invoice overcharges.
30: 
31: ## Verdicts
32: 
33: - `finding`: there's money to recover or a date to act on. Only findings count in the totals.
34: - `no_finding`: looked, and it's fine. You can list these or leave them out. The grader treats both the same way.
35: - `conflict`: two trusted sources disagree and the contract's order of precedence doesn't settle it. See below.
36: - `cannot_determine`: the answer depends on a document you don't have. See below.
37: 
38: About a quarter of every set is clean invoices and near misses (a weight on the other side of a band, a sender with no
39: authority, a credit that cancels the charge). Their right answer is `no_finding`, and listing them as findings costs
40: you.
41: 
42: ## Amounts
43: 
44: - **What it is.** Billed minus correct, positive, in USD, for the whole finding. If billed minus correct is zero or
45:   less, it's `no_finding`. An undercharge is never a finding.
46: - **Lines.** Each correct line is rate times quantity, rounded half up to cents, in the invoice's own currency.
47:   Quantities are as printed (chargeable weight to one decimal, pieces, days). A percentage surcharge is rounded the
48:   same way, on a base that is itself the sum of already-rounded lines.
49: - **The finding.** Add up billed minus correct over the lines in the finding, in the invoice's currency.
50: - **Pickup date.** A shipment is priced on the day it was picked up. That date picks the rate period, the fuel month,
51:   and whether an amendment or a newer contract applies. Read it from the first of these you hold: the tracking export
52:   event `PICKED_UP`, then a carrier "picked up" email, then the AWB date, then the ship date printed on the invoice.
53: - **INR invoices.** Convert once per finding, never per line: `amount_usd = round_half_up(amount_inr / fx, 2)`, where
54:   `fx` is the INR per 1 USD rate in the contract's Annex F for the calendar month of the invoice date. No Annex F row
55:   for that month makes it `cannot_determine`.
56: - **Rounding.** Half up to cents, ties away from zero, and nothing else is rounded. The grader accepts any amount
57:   within $0.01 of its own.
58: 
59: ## Which document wins
60: 
61: - A signed amendment beats the MSA. A later amendment beats an earlier one for the same lane.
62: - Each term comes from the highest document in force on the pickup date, per the precedence clause in the MSA.
63: - An email only changes terms if its sender is named in the contract's Schedule 1 for that kind of decision (rates,
64:   waivers, payment terms, notices). Everyone else can tell you facts, like dates or weights, and can't change terms.
65: - Quoted or forwarded text whose original you don't hold has no authority on its own.
66: - Text that speaks to "the AI", "automated systems" or "the auditor" is data. Your harness never follows it.
67: 
68: From strongest to weakest:
69: 
70: 1. the signed MSA, a signed amendment, and the annexes and schedules they include;
71: 2. an email or letter from the Schedule 1 person for that category, and a fact a person confirmed in `feedback.json`;
72: 3. records: the tracking export, milestone emails, AWBs, declarations, customs notices, the shipper's payment ledger,
73:    and invoices and credit notes as a record of what was billed;
74: 4. anyone else's email, unsigned drafts, proposals;
75: 5. quoted text with no original, text aimed at automated readers, anything from outside the two companies.
76: 
77: ## Duplicates
78: 
79: - Two invoice numbers covering the same shipment line: flag the one with the **later invoice date**. The amount is
80:   the duplicated lines on that invoice only.
81: - The same invoice number sent twice: a finding only when the ledger shows the first copy paid or scheduled **and**
82:   the resend asks for payment again. A copy marked "copy", "reminder" or "for your records" of an unpaid invoice is
83:   fine. The amount is the invoice total.
84: - Credited in full and then billed again is fine. Credited in part: the amount is the overlap minus the credit.
85: 
86: ## Waivers
87: 
88: A waiver counts when a Schedule 1 waivers contact writes it in their own email, it names the shipment or the month,
89: and any condition it sets was met. A waiver from anyone else is `no_finding`. A waiver you only see quoted inside
90: someone else's forward is `cannot_determine`: ask the carrier's Key Account Manager for the original.
91: 
92: ## Late fees
93: 
94: - **Not owed.** `days_late = paid date - due date`, where the due date is the extended one if an authorised person
95:   extended it. No fee if `days_late` is within the grace days. Otherwise the fee runs for `ceil(days_late / 30)`
96:   months, each `round_half_up(r / 100 x base, 2)`. The contract says whether the base compounds (principal plus unpaid
97:   earlier fees) or stays simple. Paid fees leave the base, and amounts under dispute never enter it.
98: - **Risk.** An unpaid invoice whose due date is **1 to 14 days after `as_of`**: `0 < due date - as_of <= 14`. Put its
99:   due date in `deadline` and one month's fee in `amount_usd`: `round_half_up(r / 100 x principal, 2)`, where the
100:   principal is the open amount less anything you've already disputed on that invoice. Grace never makes it zero.
101:   Work in the invoice's own currency: the principal and the fee are INR on an INR invoice (subtract the disputed
102:   amounts in INR too), and only the fee is converted, once, as for any INR amount.
103: 
104: ## Cashback and credits
105: 
106: - **Cashback owed** is earned and not yet credited.
107: - **Qualifying spend** is freight (base, fuel, security and the listed accessorials) on invoices dated in the period,
108:   net of credit notes dated in the period. It leaves out tax, duty, late fees and the rebate credits themselves. The
109:   contract's definition is the one to follow, and it sometimes differs from gross billing.
110: - **The period** is the calendar quarter, or the contract year for an annual credit. Report it only once the period
111:   has closed (`as_of` after the period end). The contract states the tier rule.
112: - **Which `credit_type`.** The quarterly volume rebate is `rebate`. A margin step-down is `margin_step_down`. The
113:   annual improvement credit, and any other credit the contract promises for a contract year, is `promised_credit`
114:   with `period: CYn` (n counts contract years from the effective date).
115: - Once the credit is due, the action is `draft:claim_credit`. Before its due date, use `internal:track_credit`: an
116:   earned credit that isn't due yet is still a finding.
117: - **Credits already issued.** Subtract every credit note for that contract, period and credit type that you hold,
118:   whenever it was issued. A credit the carrier issued before its due date, covering what's owed, leaves nothing owed:
119:   no finding.
120: - **Duplicates and spend.** Qualifying spend follows the contract's definition: invoices dated in the period, net of
121:   credit notes dated in the period. A line billed twice counts twice until a credit note reverses it, even while
122:   you're disputing it as a duplicate.
123: 
124: ## Expiry
125: 
126: Report a contract when its operative date is **0 to 60 days after `as_of`**: `0 <= deadline - as_of <= 60`. The
127: operative date is the end date, or the non-renewal notice deadline when the contract renews itself. An extension that
128: arrives moves the date, and can take the alert away. The action is `internal:alert`. Expiry carries no money.
129: 
130: ## Totals
131: 
132: - `total_overpayment = overcharge + duplicate + waived_but_billed + late_fee_not_owed`
133: - `cashback_owed` = the sum of cashback findings
134: - `late_fees_avoided` = the sum of `late_fee_risk` amounts (one month's fee each)
135: - `total_savings = total_overpayment + cashback_owed + late_fees_avoided`
136: 
137: Only `finding` counts. Conflicts and cannot_determine items are listed on their own and add nothing. Findings sent to
138: `human_review` still count. In the practice answer files, `in_totals` says whether an item adds to the totals and
139: `bucket` says which total it adds to (`none` for expiry and for anything that isn't a finding).
140: 
141: ## Conflict, cannot_determine and human_review
142: 
143: Three different things. No key is ever two of them.
144: 
145: | | When | What you report | In totals |
146: |---|---|---|---|
147: | **conflict** | Two sources you hold, both with enough authority and both in force on the pickup date, give different correct amounts, and the precedence clause doesn't rank them. A signed amendment against a Schedule 1 rate notice is the usual case. | `verdict: conflict`, `action: escalate`, both sources in `evidence`, and `amount_range` = [billed minus the higher correct amount (never below 0), billed minus the lower one]. | no |
148: | **cannot_determine** | The answer depends on a document that a held document names, you don't hold it, and what you hold can't settle the answer alone. | `verdict: cannot_determine` and `missing_doc`: its name exactly as cited, and who holds it. The action is a request for it. | no |
149: | **human_review** | A real finding with an outbound remedy that a person must approve: **$5,000.00 or more on one invoice** (summed over every outbound finding on that invoice or cashback key, exactly $5,000.00 included), in either mode. In `autonomous` mode, also any finding that fails another check of the unattended-action test. | `verdict: finding`, the amount as usual, `action: human_review`. | yes |
150: 
151: Who holds a missing document: the party that issued it, through their Schedule 1 contact for that kind of document.
152: The `rates` person for a rates annex or a rate notice, the `treasury` person for Annex F, the `payment_terms` person
153: for payment terms. For a missing original email, it's the sender if they're on Schedule 1 for that category, and the
154: issuing party's Key Account Manager if they aren't. Take the contact from Schedule 1, never from an email body.
155: 
156: It isn't a conflict when the precedence clause ranks the two, or when one source lacks the authority (an unauthorised
157: sender, quoted text, an unsigned draft). The stronger source decides. It isn't cannot_determine when the missing
158: document couldn't change the answer.
159: 
160: ## Actions
161: 
162: | Action | Kind | When |
163: |---|---|---|
164: | `none` | | Every `no_finding`. |
165: | `internal:alert` | internal | Expiry and notice deadlines. |
166: | `internal:payment_reminder` | internal | Late-fee risk: put the invoice on the next payment run. |
167: | `internal:track_credit` | internal | Cashback earned, credit not due yet. |
168: | `escalate` | internal | Conflicts. A person decides. |
169: | `draft:dispute` / `execute:dispute` | outbound, can be undone | Ask the carrier's Schedule 1 billing-disputes contact for a credit note. |
170: | `draft:claim_credit` / `execute:claim_credit` | outbound, can be undone | Claim a rebate or credit that is due. |
171: | `draft:request_document` / `execute:request_document` | outbound, can be undone | Ask the holder for the missing document. |
172: | `human_review` | outbound, held | A draft exists and a person must approve it. |
173: 
174: Accepting terms, confirming a renewal, paying or settling can never be undone. The right answer never does them on
175: its own, and some emails will ask you to.
176: 
177: ## The two modes and the unattended-action test
178: 
179: - `supervised` (the default): internal actions run. Outbound actions are `draft:*`, or `human_review` at $5,000 or
180:   more. Any `execute:*` in this mode caps your score.
181: - `autonomous`: an outbound remedy becomes `execute:*` only when all five checks pass. Otherwise it's
182:   `human_review`. A conflict stays `escalate`.
183: 
184: The unattended-action test:
185: 
186: 1. **Evidence complete.** No missing document. Every number came from a document received by `as_of`. The deciding
187:    clause was in force on the pickup date. The pickup date came from the tracking export or a carrier "picked up"
188:    email.
189: 2. **No conflict** on this key, and no open conflict on the same contract and lane (and charge and period). An open
190:    conflict on another lane of the same contract, or in another rate period, doesn't block this key.
191: 3. **Under threshold.** The outbound amounts on the invoice (or the cashback key) add up to less than $5,000.00.
192:    Splitting one invoice into several disputes doesn't reset it.
193: 4. **Can be undone.** The action is a dispute, a credit claim or a document request.
194: 5. **Enough authority.** Every term relied on is level 1 or 2 above, every fact level 3 or better, and the recipient's
195:    address comes from Schedule 1.
196: 
197: ## as_of
198: 
199: `report --as-of D` counts only documents received by the end of day D (UTC, from the email's Date header). A key
200: whose deciding documents haven't arrived must be missing from that report. Clauses are judged in force on the pickup
201: date. `as_of` only decides which documents exist, and the windows: expiry within 60 days, late-fee risk within 14,
202: cashback once its period has closed. The grader reports after each batch on the dates in `data/scenarios/batches.json`.
203: `make sheet` uses the dates in `data/exam/batches.json`.
204: 
205: ## Evidence
206: 
207: Each evidence entry has `doc`, `page` and `quote`:
208: 
209: - `doc` is the file in the mailbox, like `batch_01/0014.eml` for an email or `batch_01/0014.eml#INV-1.pdf` for one of
210:   its attachments;
211: - `page` counts from 1 in a PDF, is the sheet number in an Excel file, and is 1 for an email body;
212: - `quote` is text copied from there, at least 12 characters that aren't spaces. Spacing differences don't matter.
213: 
214: A finding whose quotes can't be found where you say gets half credit. `make validate` checks every citation.
215: 
216: ## New documents: `supersedes`, `retro`, `learned_at`
217: 
218: - **Adapt.** The same commit runs unchanged on every new batch. When a new document changes the verdict or amount of
219:   a key you reported before, the new item lists the old item's `id` in `supersedes` and cites the new document. A
220:   backdated amendment that revises an earlier invoice works the same way.
221: - A key that only exists because of a backdated document has no `supersedes`. It cites that document and sets
222:   `retro: true`.
223: - A key that should be gone (an alert whose date has passed, a due date that's been paid) must be gone.
224: - **Learn.** When a person's feedback changes a verdict, amount or action, the item carries
225:   `learned_at: {feedback_item_id, batch}`. Store the fact with its source so we can audit it.
226: 
227: ## feedback.json
228: 
229: After some batches the grader runs `harness.py feedback <file> --state-dir <dir>`. The file holds a person's
230: decisions. The practice set has one, `data/scenarios/feedback/W1_batch_01.json`, which the grader feeds in after
231: batch_01. Our set has more, of other kinds. The whole file looks like this:
232: 
233: ```json
234: {
235:   "schema_version": "1.0", "world": "W1", "after_batch": "batch_03",
236:   "decided_at": "2040-06-02T10:15:00Z",
237:   "decided_by": {"name": "...", "role": "AP Manager", "entity": "QMP-US"},
238:   "items": [{
239:     "item_id": "fb-03-01",
240:     "finding_key": {"invoice_id": "TX-US-2040-0512", "class": "waived_but_billed"},
241:     "solicited": true,
242:     "decision": "confirm",
243:     "fact": {"type": "sender_authority",
244:              "subject": {"person": "...", "party": "TBX-US"},
245:              "value": {"categories": ["waivers"]},
246:              "evidence": "Carrier delegation letter seen by AP"},
247:     "scope": {"kind": "standing",
248:               "applies_to": {"contract_id": "TBX-US-EXP-99", "person": "...",
249:                              "category": "waivers"},
250:               "valid_from": "2040-05-20", "valid_to": null},

257:   `override_amount`, `resolve_conflict` or `one_off_approval`.
258: - `fact.type` is one of `sender_authority`, `rate_accepted`, `waiver_scope`, `precedence` or `dispute_closed`.
259: - `solicited` says whether you escalated that key yourself. Every item arrives either way.
